questions.question: While an `await` on a database query is waiting for the result, what is the request thread doing in ASP.NET Core?
options: It is blocked until the query returns
It has returned to the thread pool and can serve other requests
It is spinning in a busy-wait loop to reduce latency
It is suspended by the OS and reserved for this request
questions.explanation: When the awaited task is incomplete, the method returns an incomplete Task and the thread goes back to the pool. A pool thread runs the continuation when the I/O completes. This is why async improves scalability.
optionNotes: That is sync-over-async (`.Result`), which async avoids.
No spinning happens; completion is signalled by the OS.
Threads are not reserved; the continuation may run on a different thread.

questions.question: What does `ConfigureAwait(false)` do?
questions.code: var data = await httpClient.GetStringAsync(url).ConfigureAwait(false);
options: Runs the HTTP call on a new background thread
Makes the call synchronous
Resumes the continuation without marshalling back to the captured SynchronizationContext
Suppresses exceptions thrown by the awaited task
questions.explanation: By default `await` captures the current SynchronizationContext (UI thread, classic ASP.NET request context) and resumes on it. `ConfigureAwait(false)` skips that, so the continuation can run on any pool thread. It is recommended in library code; in ASP.NET Core there is no SynchronizationContext, so it has no effect.
optionNotes: No thread is created by ConfigureAwait.
It is still fully asynchronous.
Exceptions still propagate normally.

questions.question: A WPF button handler calls `var x = LoadAsync().Result;` and the app freezes forever. `LoadAsync` awaits an HTTP call without `ConfigureAwait(false)`. Why?
options: HttpClient cannot be used from the UI thread
The UI thread is blocked on `.Result`, but the continuation of `LoadAsync` must run on that same UI thread
`.Result` throws an AggregateException that is swallowed
The thread pool is exhausted by the HTTP call
questions.explanation: This is the classic sync-over-async deadlock. The continuation after `await` is posted to the captured UI SynchronizationContext, which is blocked waiting for the task, so neither can proceed. Fix: make the handler `async` and `await LoadAsync()`.

questions.question: Where is an `async void` method acceptable?
options: In repository methods that don't return data
In controller actions that return no body
In event handlers such as `button_Click`
Anywhere the result isn't needed
questions.explanation: `async void` can't be awaited, and exceptions thrown from it are raised on the SynchronizationContext, typically crashing the process. It exists for event handlers whose signature must return void. Everything else should return `Task`.

questions.question: Two independent HTTP calls each take about 300 ms. How long does this method take, roughly?
questions.code:
var a = await GetPriceAsync();
var b = await GetStockAsync();
options: It depends on the number of CPU cores
questions.explanation: Each call starts only after the previous one finishes, so they run sequentially. Start both first and then `await Task.WhenAll(priceTask, stockTask)` to bring it down to roughly 300 ms.

questions.question: Which statements about `ValueTask<T>` are true? (Select all that apply)
options: It can avoid a heap allocation when the result is available synchronously
It is safe to await the same instance multiple times
It should be awaited exactly once
It should replace `Task<T>` in all public APIs
questions.explanation: `ValueTask<T>` is a struct that can carry a result directly, avoiding an allocation on synchronous completion. It may be backed by a pooled `IValueTaskSource`, so awaiting twice or after completion is undefined. Use it only on hot paths after measuring; `Task<T>` remains the default.
optionNotes: Pooled sources may be reused after the first await.
It adds constraints for callers; Task stays the default.

questions.question: How does exception behaviour differ between `task.Result` and `await task` when the task faults?
options: Both throw the original exception
`.Result` throws an AggregateException wrapping it; `await` rethrows the first inner exception directly
`await` throws AggregateException; `.Result` throws the original
Neither throws; you must inspect `task.Exception`
questions.explanation: Blocking accessors (`.Result`, `.Wait()`) wrap failures in `AggregateException`. `await` unwraps and rethrows the first inner exception while preserving its stack trace, which is far easier to catch and log.

questions.question: In an ASP.NET Core controller, a developer wraps a database call in `await Task.Run(() => repo.GetAll())` "to make it async". What is the effect?
options: Better throughput, because the request thread is freed
No scalability gain: it just moves the blocking work to another pool thread and adds overhead
It deadlocks because ASP.NET Core has a SynchronizationContext
The query runs in parallel across multiple cores
questions.explanation: The request thread is freed, but another pool thread is now blocked doing the synchronous I/O, so pool usage is the same plus scheduling overhead. The fix is a truly async API such as `ToListAsync()`. `Task.Run` is for offloading CPU work from a UI thread.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of passing a `CancellationToken` through async calls in a Web API?
options: To make the method run faster
To let downstream work stop when the client disconnects or a timeout fires
To prevent deadlocks
It is required for the method to compile
questions.explanation: ASP.NET Core exposes `HttpContext.RequestAborted`. Passing it to EF Core and HttpClient lets expensive work stop when nobody is waiting for the result, which saves database and CPU resources.

questions.question: What happens when this code runs?
options: Both queries run concurrently on one connection
EF Core throws InvalidOperationException because a second operation started before the first completed
EF Core automatically queues the second query
It works but returns stale data
questions.explanation: `DbContext` is not thread-safe and does not support concurrent operations. EF Core detects this and throws "A second operation was started on this context instance before a previous operation completed". Use separate contexts (for example via `IDbContextFactory`) for parallel queries.

questions.question: What does the C# compiler (Roslyn) produce when you build a class library?
options: Native machine code for the current CPU
An assembly containing IL, metadata and a manifest
Source code for the CLR to interpret line by line
A Docker image with the runtime included
questions.explanation: Roslyn compiles C# to Intermediate Language plus metadata describing every type, packaged in an assembly (.dll). The CLR's JIT turns IL into native code at run time, unless you publish with ReadyToRun or Native AOT.
optionNotes: Only Native AOT publishing produces native code ahead of time.
IL is compiled by the JIT, not interpreted line by line.
Container images are a separate publishing step.

questions.question: In late 2026, which .NET version is the current Long-Term Support (LTS) release?
options: .NET 9
.NET 11
.NET 10
.NET 8
questions.explanation: .NET ships every November; even-numbered releases are LTS with 3 years of support. .NET 10 (November 2025) is the current LTS. .NET 11 (November 2026) is an STS release, and .NET 8 and 9 reach end of support in November 2026.
optionNotes: Odd-numbered releases are STS.
.NET 11 is an STS release.
.NET 8 was the previous LTS and its support ends in November 2026.

questions.question: A benchmark shows a method is noticeably slower during its first few dozen calls than afterwards. What runtime feature best explains this?
options: Tiered compilation: it starts as quickly compiled Tier 0 code and is later recompiled with full optimizations once hot
The garbage collector compacts the method's IL after a number of calls
The CLR interprets IL until the method has been called 100 times
ReadyToRun code is discarded after the first call
questions.explanation: Tier 0 favours fast startup with minimal optimization. Hot methods (about 30 calls, or loops via on-stack replacement) are recompiled at Tier 1, using Dynamic PGO data to devirtualize and inline. That is why benchmarks need warm-up.
optionNotes: The GC manages data, not code.
The CLR does not interpret IL; it always JIT-compiles it (or uses precompiled code).
R2R code is replaced only for hot methods, which is an optimization, not a slowdown.

questions.question: You publish an Azure Function (AWS: Lambda) API with Native AOT to cut cold starts. JSON serialization now fails or warns about trimming. What is the usual fix?
options: Switch to the Newtonsoft.Json package
Disable trimming but keep Native AOT
Call `GC.Collect()` before serializing
Use System.Text.Json source generation with a `JsonSerializerContext`
questions.explanation: Native AOT has no JIT and trims unused code, so reflection-based serialization cannot discover types at run time. The System.Text.Json source generator produces the serialization code at compile time, which is trim- and AOT-safe.
optionNotes: Newtonsoft.Json is reflection-heavy and not AOT-friendly.
Native AOT always trims; you can't simply turn it off.
Garbage collection has nothing to do with trimming.

questions.question: Which statements about ReadyToRun (R2R) publishing are true? (Select all that apply)
options: The IL is kept, so hot methods can still be re-JITted with Tier 1 optimizations
It removes the need for any .NET runtime on the target machine
It improves startup because most methods don't need JIT compilation at launch
It disables reflection, like Native AOT does
questions.explanation: R2R precompiles IL to native code but keeps the IL and the JIT, so startup improves and the runtime can still optimize hot paths. Whether you need an installed runtime depends on framework-dependent vs self-contained deployment, not on R2R. Reflection keeps working.
optionNotes: That is self-contained deployment, a separate option.
Only Native AOT restricts dynamic features.

questions.question: A shared library marked `[assembly: CLSCompliant(true)]` exposes `public uint GetCount()`. What does the compiler warn about, and why?
options: `uint` is slower than `int` on 64-bit CPUs
`uint` is not part of the Common Language Specification, so some .NET languages may not be able to consume it
`uint` is not part of the Common Type System
Public methods must return reference types to be CLS-compliant
questions.explanation: The CTS defines all runtime types, including unsigned integers. The CLS is the subset every .NET language must support, and unsigned types aren't in it. For cross-language public APIs you expose `int` or `long` instead.
optionNotes: Performance is not the concern here.
`uint` (System.UInt32) is a CTS type.
Value types like `int` are CLS-compliant return types.

questions.question: What is the unit of deployment and versioning in .NET, and also the boundary of the `internal` access modifier?
options: Namespace
Solution
Assembly
NuGet feed
questions.explanation: An assembly (.dll) carries IL, metadata and a manifest with its name and version. `internal` members are visible only within the same assembly. Namespaces are just logical naming and can span assemblies.
optionNotes: Namespaces are logical and can span many assemblies.
A solution is a build-time grouping of projects.
A feed distributes packages, which contain assemblies.

questions.question: A .NET Framework app loads plugins into separate AppDomains so it can unload them. When migrating to .NET 10, what replaces this?
options: Creating new AppDomains works exactly as before
The Global Assembly Cache (GAC)
Running each plugin with `Task.Run`
A collectible `AssemblyLoadContext`
questions.explanation: Modern .NET supports only a single AppDomain. `AssemblyLoadContext` provides assembly isolation, and a collectible context can be unloaded once nothing references its types. For strong isolation (security, crash containment) use separate processes.
optionNotes: Creating additional AppDomains throws PlatformNotSupportedException in modern .NET.
The GAC doesn't exist in modern .NET and never provided isolation.
Tasks share the same assemblies; there's no isolation or unloading.

questions.question: Which of these is a reference type?
options: `int`
`DateTime`
`string`
`Guid`
questions.explanation: `string` is a reference type, although it is immutable and overrides `==` to compare contents, which makes it feel like a value type. `int`, `DateTime` and `Guid` are structs.

questions.question: What does this print?
options: True, True
False, True
True, False
False, False
questions.explanation: Each assignment boxes 5 into a separate heap object. `==` on `object` compares references, so it is False. `Equals` is virtual and dispatches to `Int32.Equals`, which compares values, so it is True.
optionNotes: `==` on two `object` variables is reference equality.
`Equals` is overridden by Int32 to compare values.
`Int32.Equals` compares the boxed values.

questions.question: What does this print?
options: Compile-time error
questions.explanation: Assigning a struct copies the whole value. `p2` is an independent copy, so changing `p2.X` doesn't affect `p1`. With a class, both variables would reference the same object and it would print 10.
optionNotes: That would happen if Point were a class.
p1.X was set to 1 and never changed.
Mutating a local struct variable's field is allowed.

questions.question: What is boxing?
options: Casting a derived class to its base class
Wrapping a reference in a `Nullable<T>`
Converting a string to a number
Copying a value type into a new heap object so it can be treated as `object` or an interface
questions.explanation: Boxing allocates a heap object and copies the value into it, for example `object o = 42;`. Unboxing type-checks and copies the value back out. It costs an allocation, which is why generics replaced non-generic collections like `ArrayList`.

questions.question: What does this print?
options: True True
False False
True False
False True
questions.explanation: Records generate value-based `Equals` and `==` that compare all members, so `a == b` is True. They are still reference types and two `new` calls create two objects, so `ReferenceEquals` is False.
optionNotes: They are two separate objects.
Record `==` compares values, not references.
Reference equality can't be true while value equality is false for records.

questions.question: What happens when this runs?
questions.code:
object boxed = 42;
long value = (long)boxed;
options: `value` is 42
`InvalidCastException` at run time
Compile-time error
`OverflowException` at run time
questions.explanation: Unboxing must use the exact boxed type. The box contains an `Int32`, so unboxing to `long` throws. Write `(long)(int)boxed` (unbox, then convert) or `Convert.ToInt64(boxed)`.
optionNotes: The int-to-long conversion only works on an unboxed int.
The cast from object to long compiles; the check happens at run time.
No arithmetic overflow is involved.

questions.question: Which statements about where value types are stored are true? (Select all that apply)
options: Value types are always stored on the stack
A struct field of a class is stored inside that object on the heap
The elements of an `int[]` are stored on the stack
A local variable captured by a lambda is hoisted into a heap-allocated class
questions.explanation: A value type lives wherever its container lives. Locals are typically on the stack, but fields of classes and array elements live on the heap, and captured locals (or locals used across `await`) are hoisted into compiler-generated classes on the heap.
optionNotes: Only plain locals and parameters usually are.
Arrays are heap objects; their elements are inside them.

questions.question: `P` is a mutable struct with a public field `X`. What happens with this code?
options: The element in the list now has X = 5
It compiles but silently modifies a temporary copy
Compile-time error CS1612: cannot modify the return value because it is not a variable
It throws `InvalidOperationException` at run time
questions.explanation: The `List<T>` indexer returns a copy of the struct, so assigning to its field would change a temporary. The compiler rejects it. Arrays are different: `arr[0].X = 5` works because an array element is a variable. Prefer readonly structs to avoid the confusion.
optionNotes: The indexer returns a copy, not a reference to the element.
The compiler catches this case and reports an error.
It never compiles, so nothing runs.

questions.question: With nullable reference types enabled, how do `string` and `string?` differ at run time?
options: They don't: it is the same type, and `?` only drives compile-time warnings
`string?` is `Nullable<string>`
`string?` adds a runtime null check on every access
`string` variables can never hold null at run time
questions.explanation: Nullable reference types are annotations used by compiler flow analysis. The runtime type is `System.String` in both cases, so you still need guard clauses at API boundaries. `Nullable<T>` only applies to value types such as `int?`.
optionNotes: `Nullable<T>` requires a value type.
No runtime checks are inserted.
Callers can still pass null, e.g. via `!` or code with NRT disabled.

questions.question: How many base classes and interfaces can a C# class have?
options: Many base classes, one interface
One base class, many interfaces
One base class, one interface
Many base classes and many interfaces
questions.explanation: C# has single inheritance of implementation (one base class) but a class can implement any number of interfaces. That is one reason interfaces are used for contracts and DI.

questions.question: What does this print?
options: Base.Virt, Base.Hide
Derived.Virt, Derived.Hide
Derived.Virt, Base.Hide
Base.Virt, Derived.Hide
questions.explanation: `override` replaces the virtual slot, so the runtime type (Derived) decides. `new` hides the method with an unrelated one, so the compile-time type of the variable (Base) decides.
optionNotes: The override is used through a base reference.
Hiding with `new` doesn't participate in virtual dispatch.
Both results are reversed.

questions.question: What does `new Child()` print?
options: Parent ctor, Child.Init field null, Child ctor
Parent ctor, Parent.Init, Child ctor
Parent ctor, Child.Init field ctor, Child ctor
Parent ctor, Child.Init null null, Child ctor
questions.explanation: Derived field initializers run first, then the base constructor, then the derived constructor body. The virtual call from Parent's constructor dispatches to the override, which sees `_a` (initializer already ran) but not `_b` (set later in the body). This is why virtual calls in constructors are risky.
optionNotes: Virtual dispatch uses the runtime type even inside the base constructor.
The Child constructor body hasn't run yet, so `_b` is null.
Field initializers run before the base constructor, so `_a` is set.

questions.question: What does `protected internal` mean?
options: Accessible only from derived classes in the same assembly
Accessible only within the same file
Accessible only from the declaring class
Accessible from the same assembly, or from derived classes in any assembly
questions.explanation: `protected internal` is the union of `protected` and `internal`. Its counterpart `private protected` is the intersection: derived classes that are also in the same assembly.
optionNotes: That is `private protected`.
That is the `file` modifier, which applies to types.
That is `private`.

questions.question: Which of these can an abstract class have that an interface cannot?
options: Methods with a body
Static members
Instance fields and constructors
Members with a non-public access modifier
questions.explanation: Interfaces can't hold instance state or declare constructors. Since C# 8 they can have default method bodies, static members and private/protected members, so those no longer distinguish them from abstract classes.
optionNotes: Default interface methods (C# 8) allow bodies.
Interfaces can have static members, including static abstract ones (C# 11).
Interfaces can have private and protected members since C# 8.

questions.question: What happens with this code?
options: Prints "Hello Ann" because the class inherits the default body
Compile-time error: `Greet` is only accessible via `IGreeter`
`MissingMethodException` thrown when `Greet` is called
Compile-time error: `EnglishGreeter` must implement `Greet`
questions.explanation: A default interface method isn't inherited as a class member. The class satisfies the interface, but you can only call the default implementation through the interface type: `IGreeter g = new EnglishGreeter();`.
optionNotes: It would print this if `g` were typed as `IGreeter`.
The problem is caught at compile time.
The default body satisfies the interface requirement.

questions.question: What are real benefits of marking a class `sealed`? (Select all that apply)
options: It makes instances thread-safe
The JIT can devirtualize and inline calls more easily
It gives the class value-type copy semantics
Other code can't derive from it and depend on its internals
questions.explanation: Sealing documents that the type isn't designed for inheritance, prevents fragile subclasses, and lets the JIT turn virtual or interface calls on the sealed type into direct calls. It has no effect on thread safety or copy semantics.
optionNotes: Thread safety depends on how state is accessed.
Sealed classes are still reference types.

questions.question: Why do teams usually prefer a DI-registered singleton service over a static class holding shared state?
options: It can implement an interface, be injected, and be replaced with a fake in tests
Static classes can't contain methods
Static classes are garbage collected after every request
A DI singleton is automatically thread-safe
questions.explanation: A static class can't implement interfaces or be substituted, so code that uses it is hard to test and tightly coupled. A singleton registered in DI is a normal object behind an abstraction with a container-managed lifetime. It still needs to be thread-safe yourself.
optionNotes: Static classes contain static methods.
Statics live for the lifetime of the process.
Singletons are shared across threads, so you must make them thread-safe.

questions.question: Which of these is compile-time (static) polymorphism in C#?
options: Overriding a virtual method
Implementing an interface
Calling a method through a base-class reference
Method overloading
questions.explanation: Overloads are resolved by the compiler from the argument types. Overriding and interface implementation are resolved at run time through virtual dispatch.

questions.question: Where is a newly created small object (for example a DTO) allocated?
options: Gen 2
Large Object Heap
Gen 0
Gen 1
questions.explanation: New small objects go to Gen 0, which is collected often and cheaply because most objects die young. Survivors are promoted to Gen 1 and then Gen 2.
optionNotes: Objects reach Gen 2 only after surviving collections.
Only objects of 85,000 bytes or more go to the LOH.
Gen 1 holds survivors of a Gen 0 collection.

questions.question: What does a `using` statement on an `IDisposable` compile to?
options: A `try/finally` that calls `Dispose()` in the `finally` block
A call to `GC.Collect()` at the end of the block
A finalizer registered for the object
A `try/catch` that calls `Dispose()` only if an exception occurs
questions.explanation: The compiler emits `try { ... } finally { x?.Dispose(); }`, so cleanup runs whether the block completes normally or throws. `await using` does the same with `DisposeAsync()`.
optionNotes: `using` never triggers a garbage collection.
Finalizers are unrelated to `using`.
Dispose runs on success as well, because it's in `finally`.

questions.question: An API allocates a new `byte[200_000]` buffer for every request. Why can this hurt performance?
options: Arrays of bytes are always boxed
The array is allocated on the stack and overflows it
The buffer is collected in Gen 0 too aggressively
It lands on the Large Object Heap, which is collected only with Gen 2 and isn't compacted by default
questions.explanation: Objects of 85,000 bytes or more go to the LOH. Frequent large allocations trigger expensive full collections and fragment memory. Rent buffers from `ArrayPool<byte>.Shared` or stream the data instead.
optionNotes: Arrays are already reference types; nothing is boxed.
Arrays are heap-allocated.
Large objects never go to Gen 0.

questions.question: Why are objects with finalizers more expensive for the GC?
options: Finalizers run on the thread that allocated the object
When found dead they are queued for the finalizer thread and survive at least one more collection
They are allocated directly on the Large Object Heap
They prevent Gen 0 collections from running
questions.explanation: Finalizable objects are tracked from allocation. When unreachable they move to the f-reachable queue, get promoted, wait for the single finalizer thread, and are only freed by a later GC. `Dispose` plus `GC.SuppressFinalize` avoids this.
optionNotes: Finalizers run on a dedicated finalizer thread.
Having a finalizer doesn't change which heap is used.
Gen 0 collections still run normally.

questions.question: Memory grows steadily in a long-running service. A heap snapshot shows thousands of `PriceWidget` objects, each subscribed with `feed.PriceChanged += OnPriceChanged` to a singleton `PriceFeed`. What is the most likely cause?
options: The GC doesn't collect objects that have event handler methods
`PriceWidget` should be a struct
The singleton's event delegate holds references to every subscribed widget, keeping them reachable
Events always allocate on the Large Object Heap
questions.explanation: An event subscription stores a delegate whose target is the subscriber. As long as the long-lived publisher is reachable, so are all its subscribers. Unsubscribe with `-=` in `Dispose`, or use a weak-event approach.
optionNotes: Having handler methods doesn't prevent collection; being referenced does.
Structs wouldn't fix the reference from the delegate (and would be boxed).
Delegates are small objects.

questions.question: Which of these act as GC roots? (Select all that apply)
options: Static fields
Objects referenced only by a `WeakReference<T>`
Local variables of methods currently on a thread's stack
Every object that has been promoted to Gen 2
questions.explanation: Roots are the starting points of the mark phase: statics, live locals and registers, GC handles and the finalization queue. A weak reference deliberately doesn't keep its target alive, and a Gen 2 object is collected like any other once nothing reachable points to it.
optionNotes: Weak references don't keep targets alive.
Generation affects how often it is checked, not whether it is a root.

questions.question: A `sealed` class owns a `FileStream` field and nothing else unmanaged. What is the right cleanup design?
options: Add a finalizer that disposes the FileStream
Call `GC.Collect()` in `Dispose()` to free the file handle
Rely on the GC; FileStream closes itself eventually
Implement `IDisposable` (and `IAsyncDisposable`) that disposes the stream; no finalizer
questions.explanation: `FileStream` already wraps its OS handle in a `SafeHandle` with its own finalizer. Your class only owns a managed wrapper, so plain `Dispose`/`DisposeAsync` is enough. A finalizer would add GC cost and must not touch other managed objects anyway.
optionNotes: Finalizers shouldn't access other finalizable objects, and this adds GC overhead.
Forcing a GC is expensive and doesn't make disposal deterministic.
Waiting for finalization keeps the file locked for an unpredictable time.

questions.question: Which GC mode does an ASP.NET Core app use by default, and why?
options: Server GC: a heap and GC thread per core, optimized for throughput
Workstation non-concurrent GC: lowest memory use
No GC: ASP.NET Core uses reference counting
Workstation GC: optimized for UI responsiveness
questions.explanation: ASP.NET Core defaults to Server GC for throughput across many request threads, with background Gen 2 collections. Since .NET 9, DATAS adapts the number of heaps to the load, which helps in memory-limited containers.
optionNotes: That mode suits small tools, not servers.
.NET uses a tracing GC, not reference counting.
Workstation is the default for desktop and console apps.

questions.question: You need to check, millions of times, whether an id has been seen before. Which collection gives O(1) average membership checks?
options: `List<T>`
`SortedSet<T>`
`HashSet<T>`
`LinkedList<T>`
questions.explanation: `HashSet<T>` uses a hash table, so `Contains` and `Add` are O(1) on average. `List<T>.Contains` is O(n), and `SortedSet<T>` is O(log n).
optionNotes: `List<T>.Contains` scans linearly: O(n).
A red-black tree gives O(log n).
Linked list search is O(n).

questions.question: What happens when this runs?
options: The list becomes [1, 3] with no error
`InvalidOperationException` (collection was modified)
Only the first element is removed
The loop never terminates
questions.explanation: `List<T>` tracks a version number; the enumerator throws if the list changes during iteration. Use `nums.RemoveAll(n => n == 2)`, iterate a copy, or loop backwards with `for`.
optionNotes: That is what `RemoveAll` would give.
The enumerator detects the change and throws.
The enumerator detects the change and throws.

questions.question: `Key` overrides `GetHashCode` to return `Id` and `Equals` to compare `Id`. What does this print?
options: Throws InvalidOperationException
True
Compile-time error
False
questions.explanation: The object was stored in the bucket for hash 1. After mutation its hash is 2, so the lookup searches the wrong bucket and doesn't find it. Keys of hash-based collections must be immutable (records with init-only properties are a good fit).
optionNotes: HashSet doesn't detect mutated keys.
The lookup uses the new hash, which points to a different bucket.
This compiles fine.

questions.question: A method only needs to loop over the items it receives. Which parameter type is the best choice?
options: `IEnumerable<T>`
`List<T>`
`IList<T>`
questions.explanation: Accept the least capable interface you need. `IEnumerable<T>` lets callers pass a list, array, set or LINQ query. Requiring `List<T>` forces callers to convert.
optionNotes: Forces callers to create a List.
Asks for indexing and mutation you don't use.
Forces callers to create an array.

questions.question: Which assignment compiles?
options: `List<object> a = new List<string>();`
`IList<object> b = new List<string>();`
`IEnumerable<object> c = new List<string>();`
`List<string> d = new List<object>();`
questions.explanation: `IEnumerable<out T>` is covariant because it only produces items, so a sequence of strings is safely a sequence of objects. `List<T>` and `IList<T>` are invariant because they also accept `T` via `Add`, which would let you insert a non-string.
optionNotes: `List<T>` is invariant.
`IList<T>` is invariant because it has `Add` and a setter.
Neither variance direction allows this.

questions.question: What happens with this code?
questions.code:
object[] items = new string[2];
items[0] = 1;
options: It compiles, then throws `ArrayTypeMismatchException` at run time
Compile-time error
It stores a boxed 1 in the array
It throws `InvalidCastException` at run time
questions.explanation: Arrays of reference types are covariant (a legacy design), so `string[]` converts to `object[]`. Every store is then type-checked at run time, and writing an `int` into a `string[]` fails. Generic interfaces avoid this by allowing covariance only for read-only use (`out T`).
optionNotes: Array covariance makes the assignment legal at compile time.
The runtime check rejects the store.
The specific exception is ArrayTypeMismatchException.

questions.question: `cache.GetOrAdd(key, k => LoadFromDb(k))` on a `ConcurrentDictionary` sometimes calls `LoadFromDb` twice for the same key under load. Why, and what is the usual fix?
options: It's a bug in ConcurrentDictionary; wrap every call in `lock`
The dictionary isn't thread-safe for reads; use `Dictionary` with a lock
`GetOrAdd` removes entries under memory pressure; increase capacity
The factory runs outside the internal lock, so racing threads may each run it; store `Lazy<T>` values so the work runs once
questions.explanation: ConcurrentDictionary guarantees only one value is stored, but it doesn't hold a lock while running your factory, so concurrent callers may all execute it and the losers' results are discarded. Wrapping values in `Lazy<T>` (with ExecutionAndPublication mode) makes the expensive work run once.
optionNotes: This is documented behaviour, and a global lock kills concurrency.
Reads and writes are thread-safe.
ConcurrentDictionary doesn't evict entries.

questions.question: Which statements are true? (Select all that apply)
options: `Dictionary<K,V>` guarantees enumeration in insertion order
`SortedDictionary<K,V>` inserts in O(log n)
`LinkedList<T>` offers O(1) access by index
`List<T>.Add` is amortized O(1)
questions.explanation: `SortedDictionary` is a red-black tree, so inserts and lookups are O(log n). `List<T>.Add` is O(1) except when the backing array doubles, which averages out. Dictionary order is not guaranteed, and linked lists need O(n) to reach an index.
optionNotes: Order often looks preserved but is not guaranteed, especially after removals.
Reaching the i-th node means walking the list: O(n).

questions.question: When is `FrozenDictionary<K,V>` (.NET 8+) the right choice?
options: When many threads add and remove items concurrently
For lookup data built once (e.g. at startup) and read very often
When you need items sorted by key
When you need to modify items while enumerating
questions.explanation: Frozen collections are immutable and spend extra time at creation to optimize read performance. They suit configuration, feature flags or reference data loaded once and read on every request.
optionNotes: Use ConcurrentDictionary for concurrent writes.
Use SortedDictionary or SortedList for ordering.
Frozen collections can't be modified at all.

questions.question: Which LINQ method executes the query immediately?
options: `Where`
`Select`
`ToList`
`OrderBy`
questions.explanation: `ToList` enumerates the source and materializes the results. `Where`, `Select` and `OrderBy` are deferred: they only describe the query until something enumerates it.

questions.question: What does this print?
options: An empty line
questions.explanation: The query is deferred: it runs when `string.Join` enumerates it, after 4 was added, so it sees the current contents of the list.
optionNotes: That would require the query to run when defined.
The filter `n > 1` still applies.
The filter matches three items.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: `Where` and `Select` are streaming operators: each item flows through the whole pipeline before the next one is pulled. Item 2 fails the filter, so it never reaches `Select`.
optionNotes: That is stage-by-stage execution, which LINQ to Objects doesn't do.
Item 2 is filtered out and never reaches Select.
Select can't run before Where provides items.

questions.question: A repository method returns `IEnumerable<Order>` as `return db.Orders;`. A caller writes `repo.GetAll().Where(o => o.Id == id).FirstOrDefault()`. What happens?
options: EF Core runs a query without a WHERE clause, streams every order into memory, and filters there
EF Core generates `SELECT TOP(1) ... WHERE Id = @id`
It throws because `IEnumerable` can't be filtered
EF Core caches the whole table and filters the cache
questions.explanation: The static type is `IEnumerable<Order>`, so `Where` binds to `Enumerable.Where` with a compiled delegate. EF Core only sees the bare DbSet and fetches all rows. Return `IQueryable<T>` deliberately, or better, expose specific methods such as `FindAsync(id)`.
optionNotes: That only happens when `Where` binds to `Queryable.Where`.
Filtering IEnumerable works fine, just in memory.
EF Core doesn't cache query results like that.

questions.question: How does `Single()` differ from `First()`?
options: `Single()` returns null when nothing matches
`Single()` throws if there are zero or more than one elements
`Single()` is faster because it stops at the first match
There is no difference
questions.explanation: `First()` returns the first element and throws only on an empty sequence. `Single()` asserts exactly one element and throws otherwise, so it must look past the first match. Use it when uniqueness is an invariant.
optionNotes: That is `SingleOrDefault()` (when nothing matches).
It must check for a second match, so it can't stop at the first.
Their behaviour differs when there are several matches.

questions.question: Against EF Core and SQL Server, why is `db.Orders.Any(o => o.Status == Status.Pending)` preferred over `.Count(...) > 0`?
options: `Count` isn't supported by EF Core
`Any` loads the rows first, so it's cached
`Count` always runs on the client
`Any` translates to `EXISTS`, which can stop at the first matching row
questions.explanation: `Any` becomes `EXISTS (SELECT 1 ...)`, which SQL Server can satisfy as soon as it finds one row. `COUNT(*)` must count every matching row. The same reasoning applies in memory: `Any()` stops at the first element.
optionNotes: Count translates to COUNT(*).
Neither loads rows.
Count is translated to SQL.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: Each terminal operator re-runs the deferred query. `Count()` evaluates the predicate for all 4 items; `First()` starts again and stops after the first match, adding 1. This is the multiple-enumeration problem; against a database it means two queries.
optionNotes: Count() enumerates everything.
That ignores the second enumeration by First().
First() stops at the first matching element.

questions.question: Which of these operators use deferred execution? (Select all that apply)
options: `GroupBy`
`Count`
`Where`
`ToDictionary`
questions.explanation: `GroupBy` and `Where` return a sequence that runs when enumerated (`GroupBy` buffers the source at that point). `Count` and `ToDictionary` return a value or materialized collection, so they execute immediately. `ToLookup` is the immediate counterpart of `GroupBy`.
optionNotes: Count returns a number, so it must run now.
ToDictionary materializes immediately.

questions.question: In EF Core 10, a query's `Where` calls a C# helper method that can't be translated to SQL. What happens?
options: EF Core silently loads the table and evaluates the helper in memory
EF Core throws `InvalidOperationException` saying the expression could not be translated
The helper is ignored and all rows are returned
SQL Server raises a syntax error
questions.explanation: Since EF Core 3.0, untranslatable expressions throw instead of silently switching to client evaluation (the final `Select` projection is the exception). Rewrite the filter with translatable constructs, or deliberately call `AsEnumerable()` after filtering what you can in SQL.
optionNotes: That was EF Core 2.x behaviour and caused hidden performance problems.
EF Core never drops part of a filter.
The error happens during translation, before any SQL is sent.

questions.question: Which built-in delegate type returns a value?
options: `Action<T>`
`Func<T, TResult>`
`EventHandler`
`Action`
questions.explanation: `Func` delegates return the type given as their last type argument. `Action` delegates return `void`, and `EventHandler` is a void `(sender, args)` signature.

questions.question: What does this print?
options: Compile-time error
questions.explanation: A `for` loop has one `i` variable for the whole loop, and all three lambdas capture that same variable. By the time they run, the loop has finished with `i == 3`. `foreach` gets a fresh variable per iteration (C# 5+), so the same code with `foreach` prints 012.
optionNotes: That's the foreach behaviour, or a for loop that copies i to a local first.
The loop exits only after i becomes 3.
Capturing loop variables is legal.

questions.question: What does this print?
options: Compile-time error
questions.explanation: Both delegates in the invocation list run in order, but a multicast delegate returns only the last one's result. To collect every result, loop over `GetInvocationList()`.
optionNotes: The first result is discarded.
Results aren't combined.
Combining Func delegates with += is allowed.

questions.question: Outside the declaring class, what can you NOT do with a public `event`?
options: Subscribe with `+=`
Unsubscribe with `-=`
Subscribe a lambda
Invoke it or replace all handlers with `=`
questions.explanation: The `event` keyword limits outside code to adding and removing handlers. Only the declaring class can raise the event or reset its invocation list, which protects other subscribers. A public delegate field has no such protection.

questions.question: What does this print?
options: B
AB
A
Nothing
questions.explanation: Removal matches delegates by method and target. The lambda in the `-=` line compiles to a different method from the first lambda, so nothing is removed. Keep a reference to the handler (or use a named method) when you need to unsubscribe.
optionNotes: This would print only if the removal matched the first handler.
The B handler was added and not removed.
Both handlers are still subscribed.

questions.question: What happens when this runs?
options: Prints `13 caught boom`
Prints `13` and the exception is swallowed
Throws `AggregateException` after all three handlers run
Prints `1 caught boom`; the third handler never runs
questions.explanation: Handlers run synchronously in order. When the second throws, invocation stops and the exception propagates to the caller, so the third handler never runs. To isolate failures, iterate `GetInvocationList()` with try/catch around each call.
optionNotes: Invocation stops at the first exception.
Exceptions aren't swallowed.
Multicast invocation doesn't aggregate exceptions.

questions.question: What does this print?
options: Compile-time error: captured variables are read-only
questions.explanation: Closures capture variables, not values. The compiler moves `counter` into a display class shared by the method and the lambda, so the lambda's increments are visible to the outer code.
optionNotes: That would be true if the lambda captured a copy.
Each call increments the same variable.
Lambdas can modify captured locals (unlike Java).

questions.question: Which statements about local functions are true? (Select all that apply)
options: They must be declared above the code that calls them
They can call themselves recursively without extra setup
They cannot capture local variables
When called directly, they don't need a delegate allocation
questions.explanation: Local functions are real methods: they can be recursive, generic and declared anywhere in the enclosing method. Calling one directly needs no delegate, and captured state can live in a struct. They can capture locals unless marked `static`.
optionNotes: They can be declared after the code that uses them.
They can capture, unless declared `static`.

questions.question: Why raise an event with `PriceChanged?.Invoke(this, e)`?
options: It avoids a `NullReferenceException` when there are no subscribers, reading the field only once
It runs subscribers in parallel
It makes handlers run asynchronously
It removes subscribers that throw
questions.explanation: An event with no subscribers is null. The null-conditional operator reads the delegate once into a temporary, so another thread unsubscribing between the check and the call can't cause a null reference.
optionNotes: Handlers still run sequentially.
Invocation is synchronous.
Exceptions still propagate and nothing is removed.
